title.narrative: ILO Advancing the Decent Work Agenda in northern Africa - 2018-2025
ILO Advancing the Decent Work Agenda in northern Africa - 2018-2025

description.narrative:
Denna insats (Advancing the Decent Work Agenda in Northern Africa) är ett samarbete mellan Sida och International Labour Organisation ILO. Syftet är främja agendan för anständiga arbetsvillkor i Nordafrika. Insatsen bygger på en innovativ strategi för att främja bevisbaserad arbetsmarknadspolitik för full sysselsättning och effektiv tillgång till sociala och arbetstagarrättigheter i regionen. Insatsen ligger i linje med den svenska regeringens MENA-strategi 2016-20 (förbättrade möjligheter för regional ekonomisk utveckling som en förutsättning för fattiga människor att kunna förbättra sina levnadsvillkor) resultatområdet som berör ökad samverkan mellan länderna och arbetsmarknadens parter att verka för anständiga arbetsvillkor med fokus på social dialog och rättigheter. Insats är riktad mot länderna i Nordafrika; Marocko, Tunisien, och Egypten Internationella arbetsorganisationen (ILO) är FN:s fackorgan för sysselsättnings- och arbetslivsfrågor. ILO har som grundläggande mål att bekämpa fattigdom och befrämja social rättvisa. I uppgifterna ligger att främja sysselsättning och bättre arbetsvillkor i hela världen, samt att värna om fackliga rättigheter.ILO:s konstruktion bygger på att sammanföra regeringar med arbetstagare och arbetsgivare i en trepartisk institutionell struktur. På så sätt kan man hantera normbildning, motverka konflikter och lösa tvister med fredliga medel. Trepartsstrukturen är ILO:s unika kännemärke. Det är den enda FN-organisationen där, utöver regeringarna, aktörer i det civila samhället deltar som fullvärdiga beslutande parter i såväl styrelse som det högsta beslutande organet (Internationella arbetskonferensen, ILC).
Sida har en lång tradition av samarbete med ILO, både på global nivå men också kopplat till MENA-strategin

The aim of the intervention is to create better conditions for the job market and creation of new jobs. This is done by supporting effective implementation of international norms and regulations in the labor market - better apply the necessary labor market reforms and decisions that promote long-term sustainable job creation mechanisms. Here, issues like social protection, decent wages, dialogue between different partners in the labor market become central. The proposed intervention addresses many of the structural causes of today's labor market. The countries in the region have ratified several of the ILO Conventions but lack implementation. This effort aims to address and reduce the gap between ratification and implementation of international conventions, in order to create better conditions for people to get decent jobs. In addition, the ILO will support the countries with adequate and relevant evidence to implement appropriate labor market reforms

The Advancing the Decent Work Agenda in North Africa (ADWA) project aimed to advance the Decent Work Agenda in North Africa. The project takes an innovative approach to promote evidence based policies for full employment and effective access to International Labour Standards (ILS), including at the workplace level.
ADWA Project Phase 1: Key Pillars Outcome 1 Improved data collection, data analysis, and data use for economic policy reforms to steer towards job rich growth in target North African countries. Outcome 2 Improved ratification, reflection in national jurisprudence, enforcement and knowledge of ILSs in target North African countries. Outcome 3 Enhanced engagement of the private sector to achieve Decent Work in telecommunication and automotive sectors in target North African countries.
ADWA Project Phase 2: Key Pillars Outcome 1 Increased adoption of economic policies and reforms promoting the growth of green and inclusive jobs in partner countries. Outcome 2 Improved ratification, reflection in national jurisprudence and increased knowledge of gender related ILS in partner countries. Outcome 3 Improved contribution of the private sector to a just transition and green economy, especially from women entrepreneurs

The following summarizes a few of the main achievements under each outcome area under the concurrent two phases of the project. Some of the examples are extrapolated and analyzed from the Final Project Report.
Developmental Impact/Overall Objective Phase 1: Countries improve their capacity for economic policy reform, enhance the implementation of international labour standards and address Decent Work Deficits (including for women). Phase 2: Countries benefit from an environmentally sustainable economy characterized by decent and green jobs available to women and men on a more equal basis.
Both Morocco and Egypt made significant progress in the development of new national employment policies which have been strongly influenced by new data and analysis on employment issues. From women workers to new technologies and forms of work, to the impact of COVID19, as well as new and more robust labour and household data collection and statistical analysis conducted under ADWA. In addition, and as a result of the project, Tunisia has adapted its active labour market programming in light of the gained new monitoring and evaluation capacity. The potential for new employment in a green economic transition and opportunities for women as microentrepreneurs have been recognized and incorporated into national policies (such as Morocco's PN2E 35) and government programming (such as Tunisia's delivery of the GERME/GET Ahead training for women).
Employment Phase 1: Improved data collection, data analysis, and data use for economic policy reforms to steer towards job rich growth in target North African countries. Phase 2: Increased adoption of economic policies and reforms promoting the growth of green and inclusive jobs in partner countries ADWAs focus on supporting capacity for evidence informed policy aligned closely with partner country priorities. Governments, academic and research institutions and civil society organizations including workers and employers groups benefitted from training and assistance in adapting and implementing improved data collection and analysis tools and techniques.
Phase 1 included regional level research and the production of reports that enabled crosscountry comparisons and the use of comparable data. This in turn allowed for the rapid deployment of impact assessments on COVID19 in each country when that issue arose. The relevant statistical and analytical bodies in Egypt, Morocco and Tunisia used their improved tools and capacities, and benefitted from technical partnerships through ADWA to develop quality reports on key topics that would influence policy making, including skills and employment expenditure the impact of active labour market programmes, women's employment new forms of work labour unit costs and labour turnover, among others. These in turn directly impacted national policies: Egypt's National Employment Policy (2023), Morocco's New Development Model 202535 (2022) and Employment and Entrepreneurship Policy (PN2E 35) (2023) and Tunisia's Decree on the National Employment Fund (2022) as well as programme modifications and the launch of new services, such as those for women's entrepreneurship. More recently, mechanisms for supporting a job rich green transition have been addressed in countries, as with the use of the Just Transition Assessment Model 1 in Egypt and Tunisia and, more recently in Morocco as well as with the Morocco's new national employment strategy.
Quality of Jobs Phase 1: Improved ratification, reflection in national jurisprudence, enforcement and knowledge of ILSs in target North African countries Phase 2: Improved ratification, reflection in national jurisprudence and increased knowledge of gender related ILS in partner countries Although the majority of ILOs fundamental Conventions had been ratified by Egypt, Tunisia and Morocco before the start of the project they had limited practical impact on the quality of jobs. ADWA focused on a number of key areas in collaborating with partner countries: first to significantly increase awareness of both ILS and the reporting and supervisory functions of the standards system for those responsible, particularly parliamentarians, workers and employers organizations as well as the media.
Strategies such as joint training on reporting requirements for the social partners, as in Morocco, or parliamentary briefings, as in Egypt and Tunisia, have significantly increased knowledge and understanding of ILS. The fact that all three countries have undertaken studies on readiness for ratification of additional Conventions and are in the process of planning for ratification is significant.
This was complemented by intensive engagement with judicial systems, particularly in Egypt and Tunisia, where the responsible training authorities have incorporated ILS materials into standard training for new judges, and where additional training on ILS and gender has been developed, including (in Egypt) dedicated training for new female judges. A key new resource for judges: bench books incorporating national labour law and ILS has been produced in both Egypt and Tunisia. These innovations are having definite impacts: recent decisions by judges are citing ILS as the basis for decisions, using this to achieve an outcome better than that using existing national law alone.
Private Sector Phase 1: Enhanced engagement of the private sector to achieve Decent Work in telecom and automotive sectors in target North African countries. Phase 2: Improved contribution of the private sector to a just transition and green economy, especially from women entrepreneurs ADWAs first phase focused on two sectors, using as an entry point a large multinational company (Ericsson in Egypt and Volvo in Algeria) as a way to explore decent work deficits and opportunities for progress within the supplier chains for those industries. An analysis of OSH and decent work conditions among Ericsson suppliers was completed in 2021 to inform ongoing work in the sector, but external conditions prevented significant work from proceeding in Algeria.
The midterm evaluation recommended a different focus for this element, which led to Phase 2s concentration on the green economy, a just transition and women entrepreneurs. There has been notable progress on this even in the relatively brief scope of Phase 2. Egypt's tripartite partners have endorsed the Road Map to Responsible Business Conduct and the MNE declaration and have established an ongoing process for implementation. Morocco has incorporated principles of a green economy and just transition in its national plans. Tunisia and Morocco have both institutionalized the delivery of entrepreneurial training for women, among other achievements.
ADWAs engagement with the private sector began with its Phase 1 engagement with two major multinational firms: Ericsson, in the telecommunications industry in Egypt, and Volvo, in the automobile sector in Algeria. Signed MOUs with each company reflected their interest and engagement in advancing the decent work agenda, and led to, particularly in the case of Egypt, an extensive supply chain analysis and review of OSH issues in the sector, as well as training for Ericsson suppliers to address decent work deficits, as well as broader training on the ILOs MNE Declaration.
Nevertheless, due to a lack of response from the lead ministry and decreasing interest from Ericsson, the project adjusted the work plan and let the MoU run out in 2022. Due to the COVID19 pandemic and a decision by the Algerian Government to close the automotive sector, the work with Volvo could not take off and funds were reallocated to Outcomes 1 and 2.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
